paper_title: On the Opportunities and Challenges of Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-Model Transfer

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Prefill-to-Autoregressive Cross-model Transfer (PACT), a form of latent communication between language models, combines a larger model's prompt representations with a smaller model's efficient generation, offering a promising way to balance capability and inference cost. However, existing systems provide limited support for independently evaluating large-small model collaboration, and improved task performance alone does not establish whether the receiver benefits from the sender's information. We introduce PLatour, an open-source PACT framework that connects frozen models through lightweight, zero-initialized linear bridges trained directly with task rewards and supports hybrid-attention architectures. PLatour significantly outperforms open-source baselines on generation tasks and surpasses Mostik's reported results on shared mathematics and coding benchmarks using a substantially smaller sender. However, controlled experiments show that the gains on some tasks can be reproduced by uninformative sender signals, self-communication, or receiver-only training. We find that trainable bridges can act as parameter-efficient adaptation mechanisms without exploiting useful sender information. We therefore propose PACT-Check to quantify how much of a trained PACT system's gain genuinely comes from communication. Finally, we discuss the opportunities and challenges of PACT systems. Code is available at https://github.com/zhenyi4/platour.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models offer strong capabilities but incur substantial computational and memory costs during decoding. Smaller models are more efficient to deploy but often struggle with complex tasks or lengthy instructions. PACT (PrefilltoAutoregressive Cross-model Transfer), form of latent communication (Mostik, 2026; Ye et al., 2025; Zou et al., 2026; Castin et al., 2026), addresses this 1 trade-off by dividing computation between large sender and small receiver. The sender processes the input prompt during prefilling and transfers its internal representations to the receiver, which then generates the response independently. By limiting the senders involvement to the prefill stage, PACT aims to leverage the capability of larger models while reducing decoding latency. This approach is also compatible with existing prefilldecode disaggregated serving infrastructure (Patel et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2024). Recent results demonstrate its promise. For example, Mostik (2026) report closing 47% of the performance gap between 753Bparameter sender and 4B-parameter receiver on mathematical reasoning and coding tasks. However, Mostik remains closed-source, limiting reproduction and systematic investigation of its approach. Existing open-source methods (Fu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Castin et al., 2026) provide only limited understanding of PACTs potential, leaving open questions about how its benefits scale with generation length and senderreceiver capacity gaps, and whether the approach extends to hybrid-attention architectures and larger scales. Therefore, we introduce PLatour (Prefill-only LATent cOmmUnication for Reasoning), an opensource, simple, and scalable framework for PACT. PLatour directly optimizes the bridged system with reinforcement learning (RL), eliminating the need for the alignmentor distillation-based training commonly adopted in prior work. It connects layers at corresponding relative depths in the sender and receiver through simple, zero-initialized linear projections, avoiding complex bridge architectures. Unlike approaches that couple models through their keyvalue (KV) caches, PLatour directly transfers hidden states, enabling compatibility with hybridattention architectures. Beyond the framework itself, we provide detailed ablation studies of key design choices and share the resulting insights. (a) PLatour consistently outperforms the open-source C2C (Fu et al., 2026) across all generation tasks and surpasses the closedsource Mostik on math and coding, despite using much smaller sender. (b) Superior benchmark performance does not necessarily imply effective information transfer from the sender. PACT-Check examines whether these gains depend on sender information through inference-time interventions and separately trained controls. On Chemistry, PLatour substantially outperforms all four sanity checks, providing evidence of meaningful information transfer. In contrast, on GSM8K, all four checks achieve comparable performance, suggesting that PLatours large gain there cannot be attributed to task-specific information from the sender. dation for systematically investigating both the potential and limitations of PACT. PLatour outperforms existing open-source methods on generation tasks, supporting generation budgets of up to 16K tokens and senderreceiver parameter ratios exceeding 100:1 (Figure 1a). On benchmarks shared with the closed-source Mostik, PLatour surpasses its reported performance on mathematical reasoning and coding tasks, despite using substantially smaller sender (35B vs. 753B parameters). However, further investigation reveals more nuanced picture. Replacing sender representations with question-independent signals or independently training the receiver with reinforcement learning substantially reduces performance relative to PLatour on some tasks, but achieves comparable performance on others, including some mathematical reasoning settings (Figure 1b). These observations suggest that gains over the standalone receiver may reflect useful sender information, receiver-side adaptation, or both. Performance improvements alone therefore do not establish the contribution of cross-model information transfer. This raises fundamental question: When do PACTs gains depend on information transferred during prefill? frozen backbones. We then introduce PACT-Check, controlled evaluation protocol that combines interventions on sender information with adaptation baselines. Applied across tasks and training settings, PACT-Check identifies where PACT retains gains beyond the tested controls and where adaptation can reproduce the observed improvements, providing task-dependent evidence of the contribution of sender information. Together, these findings highlight the opportunities and challenges of PACT, while PACT-Check provides framework for more rigorous evaluation of cross-model latent communication. Our contributions are threefold. We introduce PLatour, lightweight hiddenstate-bridging PACT framework trained directly with RL, demonstrating its scalability to large senderreceiver capacity gaps, long-form generation scenarios, and hybridattention architectures. PLatour significantly outperforms existing open-source methods on generation tasks and achieves results competitive with the closedsource Mostik while using much smaller sender, making it strong baseline. To address this question empirically, we first connect PACT bridges to prefix tuning (Li and Liang, 2021) and adapters (Houlsby et al., 2019), revealing their capacity for adaptation even with Through controlled experiments, we show that comparable gains can arise without useful sender information, challenging their attribution to genuine information transfer. Based on 2 these findings, we propose PACT-Check, an evaluation protocol with four sanity checks, and PACT-Score, which measures the performance gain over the strongest control, to support rigorous evaluation of future PACT systems. We further identify open challenges and opportunities for future research.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Latent Communication. Latent communication enables models to exchange continuous representations, including soft embeddings (Pham et al., 2024), intermediate activations (Ramesh and Li, 2025), and KV caches. Interlat generates and compresses hidden-state messages (Du et al., 2026), while LatentMAS combines autoregressive latent reasoning with KV-memory transfer (Zou et al., 2026). KVComm reuses caches across agent-specific contexts to reduce redundant prefilling (Ye et al., 2025). For heterogeneous models, C2C learns task-supervised KV fusion (Fu et al., 2026), later made lightweight with shared low-dimensional bottleneck (Rossi et al., 2026), while other approaches learn shared KV spaces or generation-oriented cache transformations (Dery et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). KV-Lingo and growing line of cross-model KV transfer methods instead translate caches for model switching without re-prefilling (Castin et al., 2026; Heo et al., 2026; Qu et al., 2026; Qiu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Yun et al., 2026), optionally recomputing selected tokens (Sarkar et al., 2026) or porting the recurrent states of hybrid models (Villani, 2026); these methods treat the senders cache as substitute for the receivers own prefill and are evaluated by fidelity to it. Within this landscape, PACT restricts the larger sender to prompt encoding and assigns all subsequent autoregressive generation to smaller receiver, aiming to improve the trade-off between performance and inference efficiency. PLatour follows this division through multi-layer residual injection of sender-prefill hidden states, training the bridge with task rewards. Beyond bridge design, prior work (Zhang and Emu, 2026; Cheng et al., 2026) has investigated whether latent communication systems benefit from sender-provided information through inference-time interventions with model parameters held fixed. PACT-Check focuses on PACT systems with trainable bridges, complementing such interventions with separately trained receiver-only and self-communication controls to assess whether the observed gains can be reproduced through receiver-side adaptation. Common Representation Space. Studies of representational similarity reveal common structure across independently trained networks (Kornblith et al., 2019), while the Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that increasingly capable models may converge toward shared representational geometry (Huh et al., 2024). Work on latent-space alignment demonstrates that simple transformations can translate representations between pretrained models (Maiorca et al., 2023; Lähner and Moeller, 2024). Relative representations further enable zero-shot model stitching through similarities to shared anchors (Moschella et al., 2023). For language models, KV cache alignment learns shared cache representation space to support communication between heterogeneous models (Dery et al., 2026). PLatour enables communication between frozen language models by learning only linear projectors that map sender-prefill features to receiver residual updates. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning. Parameterefficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adapts pretrained models by optimizing small number of additional or selected parameters while keeping most pretrained weights fixed. Prefix tuning learns continuous prefix activations shared across examples to condition generation (Li and Liang, 2021), while adapter tuning introduces residual transformations of hidden states (Houlsby et al., 2019). PLatour connects to both approaches: trainable question-independent sender signals resemble learned prefixes, while selfcommunication reduces to linear residual adapter when sender and receiver use the same hidden state. unified view connects adapters, prefix tuning, and LoRA as different forms of learned hiddenstate modifications (He et al., 2022). This perspective motivates comparing PLatour with receiverside PEFT baselines such as LoRA (Hu et al., 2022). Together with sender-independent controls, these comparisons help assess whether bridging gains require useful sender information or can be explained by receiver adaptation.

sections.title: 4.1 Bridge Architecture
sections.content: For given prompt x, our goal is to learn bridge parameters ϕ that transfer useful information from the sender into the receivers state, yielding higher expected task reward than the standalone receiver: EypPACT(x;ϕ)[r(x, y)] > EypR(x)[r(x, y)], (3) where r(x, y) is the task reward and pR( x) denotes the standalone receivers generation distribution without sender communication.

sections.title: 3.2 Shared Representation Hypothesis
sections.content: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (Huh et al., 2024) suggests that independently trained models may develop similar relational structures in their representations, despite differences in architecture, training data, and capacity. OPRD (Yang et al., 2026) further reports high cosine similarity between models hidden-state representations after projection into shared low-rank space. Together, these findings motivate our hypothesis that representations at corresponding sender and receiver layers share common structure that can facilitate cross-model latent communication. Such structural similarity, however, does not guarantee effective information transfer. The sender must provide task-relevant information in form that the receiver can exploit during generation. We therefore view shared representational structure as starting point for designing communication bridges, while treating their ability to transfer useful information as an empirical question.

Communication is therefore restricted to the prefill stage. We adopt residual addition (Fu et al., 2026) rather than replacing the receivers hidden states with projected sender representations. Zero initialization preserves the standalone receivers computation before training. Its benefits are supported by the direct-GRPO initialization trajectories in Table A15 and the SFT comparisons in Table A14. LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) adopts the same initialization principle. Direct replacement does not provide this initialization property and may require an additional alignment stage. We use linear projectors instead of nonlinear MLPs to simplify the communication mechanism and facilitate its analysis. sections.title: 4.2 Training Objective
sections.content: We freeze sender and receiver and optimize only the communication bridge using GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), without preceding SFT alignment or distillation warm-up. PLatour directly maximizes the receivers expected task reward, EypPACT(x;ϕ)[r(x, y)]. We do not explicitly align sender and receiver hidden representations, since representational agreement alone does not ensure the preservation of task-relevant information. As an extreme example, an unconstrained two-sided alignment objective admits trivial solution in which both projected representations collapse to zero, achieving perfect agreement while conveying no extra information from the sender. We also avoid training the bridged receiver to imitate the senders output distribution. large capacity gap may make such imitation difficult or may even degrade the receivers performance, consistent with reported challenges in large-to-small on-policy distillation (Li et al., 2026a). Instead, we view the senders hidden states as latent tools and train the bridge to make these representations useful for maximizing the receivers generation reward.

sections.title: 5 PACT-Check
sections.content: PLatour optimizes its bridge using task rewards without explicitly requiring the receiver to use sender information. Although both model backbones remain frozen, the trainable bridge can modify the receivers computation. Gains over the standalone receiver may therefore arise from useful 5 information transfer, receiver-side adaptation, or both. To investigate these contributions, we introduce PACT-Check, an evaluation protocol comprising Dummy Transfer (DT), Irrelevant Transfer (IT), Self-Communication (SC), and Trained Receiver (TR). DT and IT are inference-only interventions that test trained systems dependence on inputspecific sender information. SC and TR require separate training runs and assess whether gains can be achieved through adaptation without an external sender. More details are in Appendix B.7. Dummy Transfer (DT). DT retains only fixed template-level sender features, removing questiondependent communication. It tests how much of the original gain persists without input-specific sender information. Retaining comparable gains suggests that question-specific sender representations may not be necessary for the observed improvement. Instead, the bridge may act as learned adaptation mechanism, potentially conditioning its effects on the receivers own representations. Irrelevant Transfer (IT). IT extends DT by injecting sender representations of tokens from an unrelated question, while the receiver continues to process the original question. It tests whether performance depends on the relevance of the transferred content. substantial drop indicates sensitivity to mismatched sender information, although such sensitivity alone does not establish semantic understanding or useful information transfer. Self-Communication (SC). SC uses the receiver model as both sender and receiver and trains the communication modules. When the transferred signal is the receivers current hidden state, with identity layer matching, Eq. 4 reduces to ℓ,t = (cid:0)I + atWℓ (cid:101)hR (cid:1)hR ℓ,t. (6) In this case, the bridge acts as linear residual adapter, connecting SC to parameter-efficient finetuning (Houlsby et al., 2019). SC therefore tests whether comparable gains can be obtained through the communication modules adaptation capacity without larger sender. Trained Receiver (TR). TR directly adapts the receiver using LoRA or full-parameter fine-tuning with SFT or GRPO. It provides reference for the gains achievable through receiver-only adaptation under these standard training protocols. PACT-Score. We define PACT-Score as the accuracy margin of PACT system over its strongest applicable PACT-Check control: PACT-Score = APACT max cC Ac, (7) where APACT is the PACT systems accuracy, Ac is the accuracy of control c, and contains the applicable controls among DT, IT, SC, and TR. positive score provides evidence for benefit from sender information. non-positive score indicates that at least one control matches or exceeds the PACT systems performance, so its gains cannot be uniquely attributed to useful sender information.

sections.title: 6 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate PLatour in two complementary settings. First, we use the Qwen3 family (Yang et al., 2025) to compare communication interfaces and training objectives under full-attention architecture, which is compatible with existing KVbased baselines. Second, we use Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026) to evaluate compatibility with hybridattention architectures and performance on harder mathematics and coding benchmarks, including comparisons with Mostiks reported results. Across these settings, PACT-Check assesses whether performance gains depend on useful sender information or can be reproduced through receiver-side adaptation. Datasets. We study latent communication on both answer-only and generation tasks. For answeronly tasks, we use ARC-C (Clark et al., 2018), MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a), and Chemistry L3 from SciKnowEval (Feng et al., 2025). We use the official ARC-C training and test splits, sample 10,000 MMLU training examples and evaluate on MMLU-Redux (Gema et al., 2025), and split Chemistry L3 into training and test sets at 9:1 ratio. For generation tasks with Qwen3, we use Chemistry (Feng et al., 2025), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), and MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021b). Chemistry uses the same split as above, with chainof-thought generation enabled. Mathematical reasoning is evaluated on the official GSM8K test set and MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024). For Qwen3.5, we train separate bridged models for mathematics and coding. The mathematics model is trained on DAPO-17k (Yu et al., 2025) and evaluated on AIME 20222026, HMMT 2025 (February and November), and IMO-AnswerBench. Our 6 AIME set comprises 135 problems: AIME and II from 20222025, and AIME from 2026. We identify 55 AIME problems overlapping with the prepared DAPO data pool: 53 with training and two with validation. We report results on both the full AIME-135 set and the fixed AIME-80 subset excluding all 55 overlaps. The coding model is trained on DeepCoder (Luo et al., 2025) and evaluated on LiveCodeBench v6 (Jain et al., 2025), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021). We deduplicate DeepCoder-24k questions, exclude overlaps with the coding benchmarks and tasks without reliably checkable outputs, and split the remaining 19,074 questions into 18,873 training and 201 validation examples, keeping nearduplicate questions in the same split. All evaluations use non-thinking mode with the modelspecific sampling settings recommended by Qwen (Yang et al., 2025; Qwen Team, 2026). Baselines. We compare PLatour against 12 baselines, grouped into four categories: standalone models, existing communication methods, receiver fine-tuning, and communication controls. Table A3 summarizes their main characteristics. i) Standalone models. Receiver Alone and Sender Alone evaluate the off-the-shelf post-trained receiver and sender independently, establishing reference performance without communication. ii) Existing communication methods. We compare against three communication baselines. C2C (Fu et al., 2026) projects and fuses sender KV caches into the receivers caches using SFT. KV-Lingo (Castin et al., 2026) initializes its bridge through closed-form linear regression on 500 training examples, replaces the receivers KV caches with projected sender caches, and subsequently trains using KL-divergence objective. TextComm provides sender-generated textual guidance, rather than latent representations, to the receiver. The sender decomposes the problem without generating final solution, and its guidance is concatenated with the original question. Although TextComm requires sender-side generation and therefore falls outside the PACT setting, it provides reference for comparing textual and latent communication. Further details are given in Appendix C. We additionally include published results from Mostik (Mostik, 2026), closed-source latent communication method supporting long-form generation and large senderreceiver size gaps. Its reported results are limited to frozen GLM-5.2 sender and frozen Qwen3.5-4B receiver; we therefore treat these as reference results rather than fully controlled comparisons. iii) Receiver fine-tuning. To assess whether performance gains arise from sender communication or receiver adaptation alone, we include LoRA-SFT, Full-SFT, LoRA-GRPO, and Full-GRPO. These methods fine-tune the receiver without sender assistance, using either supervised fine-tuning or GRPO. LoRA uses rank = 128 unless otherwise specified. Full-parameter fine-tuning uses learning rate 10 times lower than its LoRA counterpart. iv) Communication controls. Self-Communication uses the receiver as both sender and receiver, testing whether gains require cross-model communication. Virtual Sender replaces external sender representations with randomly initialized, trainable tensors, testing whether improvements depend on information supplied by an external model. Proposed method and variant. PLatour projects sender hidden states into the receivers residual stream during prompt processing and optimizes the projectors using GRPO, while keeping both model backbones frozen. PLatour-SFT uses the same architecture but trains the projectors with SFT, isolating the effect of the optimization objective. Training protocol. All SFT-based methods except KV-Lingo use labeled responses for answer-only tasks and unfiltered sender-generated rollouts on training questions for generation tasks. By design, KV-Lingo instead trains on the receivers own rollouts. For models exceeding 100B parameters, PLatour uses their FP8 versions to reduce memory burden. We evaluate PLatour only on generation tasks, as its GRPO training relies on generated responses.

sections.title: 8 Discussion
sections.content: PLatours low PACT-Scores on several long-form generation tasks suggest that much of its observed improvement can be reproduced through adaptation without useful sender information. These findings highlight central challenge for PACT: achieving gains that depend on cross-model communication. Nevertheless, our results also identify settings where communication provides benefits beyond the tested controls, motivating further exploration. Challenges. Realizing effective prefill-time communication in PACT requires distinguishing knowledge transfer from receiver adaptation. Because trainable bridge introduces additional parameters into the receiver, reward-driven training does not inherently distinguish between improvements arising from transmitted information and those arising from the bridges own learned representations. When the receiver can improve on its own, the bridge may instead function as an adapter or learned prefix, reducing the sender to an expensive source of noise. central challenge is therefore to develop training objectives that incentivize the receiver to exploit information from the sender rather than achieving gains through adaptation alone. Equally important is designing evaluations that can reliably identify genuine transfer. This requires tasks on which the receiver has sufficient capability to exploit the transmitted information but still has substantial room for improvement and on which the sender possesses meaningful knowledge advantage, as well as careful control of test-data contamination. Otherwise, apparent gains may reflect adaptation rather than transfer, while genuine transfer may be obscured by the receivers limitations or benchmark saturation. Further challenges include generalizing PACT across model families with heterogeneous representation spaces, maintaining stable training as sender models scale, and developing mechanistic explanations of what information the bridge transmits and how the receiver uses it. 11 Opportunities. Positive PACT-Scores in some settings suggest that even simple linear bridges can facilitate useful cross-model information transfer. These findings are consistent with the possibility of shared representational structure, as suggested by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (Huh et al., 2024), but do not establish the hypothesis itself. Extending our evaluation beyond models from the same family would provide stronger test of this possibility. Beyond strong-to-weak transfer, latent communication may also benefit models of similar capacity or enable weak-to-strong transfer when their capabilities are complementary. Let and denote the sets of problems solved by the receiver and sender, respectively. Problems in represent potential opportunities for transfer, even when the sender is weaker overall. The union describes potential combined coverage, rather than guaranteed outcome of communication. Realizing this potential requires the senders complementary capabilities to be encoded in representations that the receiver can effectively exploit. Another opportunity is to explore the independent scaling of problem understanding and solution search. In PACT, we view large-model prefilling as problem understanding and small-model generation as solution search. PLatour offers an early realization of this separation. This suggests two complementary ways to scale reasoning: using larger model for better problem understanding, and allowing smaller model to search longer at lower cost. Studying these two directions could reveal new ways to push the capabilitycost Pareto frontier. further opportunity is to amortize sender computation across requests sharing long system prompt. For example, an agent harness may contain tens of thousands of tokens of reusable instructions. Sender representations of this shared prefix could be precomputed, cached, and injected during receiver prefilling, avoiding repeated sender computation for each request. Whether such prefix-only communication retains the benefits of question-specific transfer remains an empirical question. Finally, shared latent interface could offer complementary communication channel across model families. One possible approach is to select intermediate layers from different models and learn projections into common representation space. Studying which representational structures can be aligned while preserving task-relevant information could improve our understanding of model representations and inform the development of more general and efficient latent communication methods.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: We formulated Prefillto-Autoregressive Crossmodel Transfer (PACT) as distinct form of latent communication in which large sender only prefills the prompt and small receiver generates the response independently, aiming to achieve Paretooptimal trade-offs between efficiency and performance through largesmall model collaboration. We also introduced PLatour, an open-source PACT framework that serves as strong baseline. PLatour outperforms existing open-source methods on generation tasks and surpasses the reported results of the closed-source Mostik on shared math and coding benchmarks with much smaller sender. However, outperforming existing methods does not necessarily mean that the receiver benefits from information provided by the sender. To distinguish genuine information transfer from receiver adaptation, we propose PACT-Check, suite of four sanity checks that test whether PACT performance depends on question-specific information from the sender. These checks reveal substantial differences across tasks and training objectives: some gains depend on useful sender information, whereas others can largely be reproduced without it. Our findings highlight task adaptation through the trainable bridge as confounding factor in PACT systems, underscoring the need to distinguish effective information transfer from gains due to adaptation. We hope PLatour and PACT-Check will facilitate more rigorous evaluation and motivate future research on more robust and effective PACT systems.

Both backbones are frozen and remain in evaluation mode. The final sender layers are aligned with the receiver layers. At each aligned layer, separate key and value networks take concatenated sender and receiver cache features and produce gated residuals added to the receivers native cache. Communication covers the prompt excluding its final token. The communication modules use BF16, random initialization, hidden and intermediate dimensions of 1,024, and dropout of 0.1. For generation, the fused prefix cache is transferred to vLLM, which processes the final prompt token and decodes the response. Within our Transformers/vLLM integration, we compare an unpadded, sample-wise reference adapter with batched adapters using intermediate padding and tail-only padding. The official C2C implementation already supports batching; this comparison concerns our runtime adapters, all of which retain the same C2C fusion architecture. The tail-only adapter keeps prompt and response tokens contiguous and replays 1https://github.com/thu-nics/C2C 16 native receiver prefix states at each layer to preserve the reference cache semantics. We check numerical consistency against the sample-wise adapter, including FP32 loss and gradient comparisons. Table A1 reports the GSM8K comparison under matched data and training settings. In this single-run comparison, tail-only padding achieves accuracy close to the sample-wise reference and higher than the intermediate-padding variant. All values are percentages. Runs share the same data, split, layer mapping, three-epoch schedule, batch size of 64, learning rate of 104, and response limit of 2,048 tokens. A.3 KV-Lingo We implement the linear, head-mixing variant of KV-Lingo (Castin et al., 2026). Both backbones are frozen and remain in evaluation mode. The final sender layers are aligned with the receiver layers. Each receiver layer has separate bias-free linear maps for keys and values, allowing information to mix across heads. Keys are translated before key normalization and rotary positional embedding (RoPE); the receivers own key normalization and RoPE are applied afterward. Translation covers the prompt excluding its final token. Training consists of two stages. First, we initialize the maps by closed-form least-squares fitting on 500 training prompts, excluding held-out examples. We accumulate sufficient statistics in FP64 and solve using pseudoinverse with relative tolerance 108. Translator parameters and projection computations use FP32, with translated states cast to the receivers BF16 dtype. Second, we optimize only the translator for three epochs using full-vocabulary KL divergence, DKL(pnativeptranslated), between the receivers continuation distributions under its native and translated caches. Both paths use the same teacher-forced continuation. The loss is averaged over continuation tokens within each example and then over examples; no cross-entropy term is added. We use AdamW with learning rate 104, batch size 64, zero weight decay, 5% warmup followed by cosine decay, and gradient-norm clipping at 1. For generation, the receiver processes the final prompt token using the translated prefix cache and continues autoregressively. Our shared evaluation pipeline transfers translated caches to vLLM for decoding. The implementation and task-specific configurations are available in our open-source code.

Table A2 summarizes the data partitions. For Qwen3 supervised experiments, we reserve approximately 1% of each training pool as an internal holdout using seed 42 and reuse the question partitions across all methods. ARC-C. We use the official ARC-Challenge splits (Clark et al., 2018), with 1,119 training and 1,172 test questions. The training set is divided into 1,107 training and 12 held-out examples. We select 10,000 unique questions from the MMLU auxiliary training set (Hendrycks et al., 2021a), excluding normalized question overlaps with MMLU-Redux 2.0 and prompts exceeding 1,024 tokens. Evaluation uses MMLU-Redux 2.0 (Gema et al., 2025): we apply available label corrections and exclude entries marked no_correct_answer or expert, retaining 5,632 questions across 57 subjects. Supervision uses the correct answer option without rationale. 17 Chemistry. We use the SciKnowEval Chemistry L3 subset (Feng et al., 2025) with the 1,890/210 train/test partition distributed with SDPO (Hübotter et al., 2026). The CoT and no-CoT settings share the same question partitions. No-CoT supervision uses the correct answer option, whereas CoT supervision uses one sender-generated reasoning trajectory per training question. GSM8K and MATH. For GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), we use the official 7,473 training and 1,319 test questions. For MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021b), we use 7,500 training problems and evaluate on MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024). Supervised training uses one sender-generated solution per question. After deduplicating normalized prompts and excluding seven questions with conflicting labels, we retain 17,391 unique problems. We reserve 500 problems for validation using seed 42 and train on the remaining 16,891. External evaluation uses AIME (135 problems), HMMT 2025 (60), and IMO-AnswerBench v2 (400). We identify 55 AIME problems overlapping with DAPO and additionally report results on the remaining 80-problem AIME subset after removing these overlaps. DeepCoder. We use DeepCoder-Preview (Luo et al., 2025), excluding problems with unsupported checker contracts. The prepared partition contains 18,873 training and 201 validation problems. All model and communication parameters remain frozen. We preserve the original layer mapping, prompts, decoding settings, response budgets, and scoring rules. The receiver always receives the original test problem, and its outputs are scored against that problems reference answer or executable tests. Dummy transfer. We replace question-dependent sender features with fixed template features computed offline. We select 500 distinct prompts from the checkpoints training pool using seed 42, excluding validation and test examples. Using prompt-only sender forwards, we compute elementwise mean features separately for each communicated layer and each fixed prefix/suffix token position. Suffix positions are aligned relative to the template suffix rather than by absolute sequence position. At inference, no sender model is loaded or called. The original communication modules transfer these fixed means only at template positions. Direct communication is disabled at question positions, padding, the final prompt token, and response positions. For PLatour, the means are computed from sender block-input hidden states before RMSNorm. For KV-based methods, keys are averaged before RoPE: C2C uses normalized keys, whereas KV-Lingo uses raw keys; both also average values. The original method-specific transformations and positional encoding are applied at the actual test positions. Irrelevant transfer. For each test problem, we select an unrelated training problem with the same fully rendered prompt-token length, including all instructions and chat-template tokens. Identical problems and known duplicates or paraphrases are excluded. Donors are selected deterministically using seed 42, with replacement, and the assignment is fixed across samples and checkpoints sharing the same protocol. When no exact-length donor is available, we rephrase only the donors wording to match the required length, preserving its problem semantics and requirements. Rewriting uses only the donor and target length, without access to the test problem or its answer. The sender processes the donor prompt, while the receiver processes the original test prompt. Donor features are transferred at all positions eligible under original transfer, including question positions. No donor solution is generated or transferred. For both controls, communication excludes the final prompt token and occurs only during prefill; subsequent decoding uses the resulting receiver cache.

sections.title: C TextComm Prompt Selection
sections.content: TextComm transmits text to the receiver instead of hidden states. The sender reads the problem and writes message, and the receiver generates the response from the problem followed by this message. Both models are frozen and run in non-thinking mode. The text baseline of C2C (Fu et al., 2026), T2T, asks the sender for one sentence of background knowledge. Before fixing the TextComm prompt, we compared T2T with four other prompts. No prompt allows the sender to solve the problem. 24 Prompts. The five prompts differ only in the sender instruction. T2T (Fu et al., 2026): the original C2C prompt, which asks for one sentence of the most essential background knowledge. Step-Back (Zheng et al., 2024): the general concepts, principles, and solution techniques required by the problem, in at most 120 words and without the specific numbers in the problem. Plan (Wang et al., 2023): plan of at most five steps that states what to compute in each step but not the results. Hint (Fu et al., 2024): the key idea, relevant formula or theorem, or useful first step. Understand: restatement of what is asked, the given conditions and implicit constraints, the relevant concepts, and likely pitfalls, in at most 150 words. Except for T2T, each prompt instructs the sender not to solve the problem, not to carry out calculations, and not to state or imply the final answer or any intermediate numerical result. The receiver prompt is: {problem} more capable assistant read this problem and left the following note (it may be incomplete and is not full solution): <note> {message} </note> followed by the answer-format instruction of the benchmark. Experimental Setup. The receiver is Qwen3.5-4B. We use two senders: Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, from the receivers model family, and GLM-5.3-Flash, from different family. The Qwen3.5-35B-A3B sender runs in non-thinking mode with =0.7, top-p=0.8, top-k=20, and presence penalty 1.5. We access GLM-5.3-Flash through OpenRouter2, where its reasoning cannot be disabled. We therefore use the lowest reasoning effort with =1.0 and top-p=0.95. Its hidden reasoning averages 40250 tokens per message across prompts and benchmarks and is not passed to the receiver. Each problem receives one message, which is shared by all receiver samples. The receiver uses the non-thinking sampling settings recommended by Qwen and the same per-sample seeds as Receiver-Alone. We select the prompt on MATH500 (avg@4, 4K-token limit) and AIME 20222026 (avg@16, 16K-token limit), with answers in boxed{}. Table A9 reports the results. Gains are measured against Receiver-Alone on the same hardware, with 95% confidence intervals from paired bootstrap over problems (5,000 resamples).

The original Qwen3-235B-A22B is no longer served, so the 235B sender is Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507, accessed through OpenRouter. On our hardware, Receiver-Alone scores 74.32 (ARC-C), 53.92 (MMLU-Redux), 39.05 (Chemistry 26 without CoT), 39.11 (Chemistry with CoT), 82.37 (GSM8K), and 72.90 (MATH500), which match Table 1 within 0.1 points on ARC-C, MMLU-Redux, and Chemistry without CoT, and within 2.3 points elsewhere. Relative to Receiver-Alone on the same hardware, TextComm improves ARC-C by 5.5 to 7.5 points and MMLU-Redux by 4.4 to 6.3 points, including with the 1.7B receiver writing to itself. It does not improve Chemistry without CoT: with note in its context, the receiver more often adds an explanation and reaches the 64-token limit. On Chemistry with CoT, it improves the receiver by 4.2 points with the 8B sender and by 1.7 points with the 235B sender. On GSM8K, the 235B and 8B senders add 7.9 and 5.8 points, respectively, and on MATH500, 3.2 and 1.5 points. Answer leakage on the Qwen3 benchmarks. On GSM8K, the senders often carry out arithmetic despite the instruction. The gold answer appears in 16 (235B), 20 (8B), and 80 (1.7B) of the 1,319 messages without appearing in the problem. Excluding these problems changes the gains by at most 0.4 points. On ARC-C, MMLU-Redux, and Chemistry, the screen flags at most 0.5% of the messages from the 235B and 8B senders. Design Evolution of PLatour: Ablation Studies In this section, we describe the design trajectory from C2C (Fu et al., 2026) to PLatour, which extends PACT from improving only multiple-choice question answering to performing well on long-form generation tasks such as MATH, AIME, and coding, while also supporting transfer to linear-attention layers. We conduct all ablation studies on MATH, using Qwen3-30B and Qwen3.5-122B as senders and Qwen3-4B and Qwen3.5-4B as receivers.

Within each ablation group, all other experimental settings are held fixed. PLatours final configurations are bolded. Hidden States or KV Caches. We first replace keyvalue (KV) caches with hidden states to make the method compatible with linear-attention layers, which allows us to run experiments with Qwen3.5 receivers in line with Mostiks setting. As shown in Table A11, hidden-state transfer even surpasses KV-cache transfer in all combinations we tried. Reward Maximization or Distillation? This is another major departure from previous methods: previous SFT-based methods degrade generation performance relative to the raw receiver, as shown 27 in Table 1. Our initial SFT variant of PLatour surpasses the raw receiver on two short-generation tasks (Chemistry and GSM8K), but still degrades performance on long-generation tasks such as MATH (Tables A11 and 1). Only GRPO consistently improves over the raw receiver by large margin. Moreover, OPD also degrades performance. These results suggest that distillation fails in the PACT setting. Our interpretation is that it is difficult for the small receiver to imitate the large senders output distribution, whereas it is easier for the receiver to leverage useful information from the sender as tool to obtain higher rewards. This key design choice enables PLatour to improve over the raw receiver on long-form generation tasks. Other Micro-Designs. We find that relative-depth layer match performs the best, and requiring fullattention receiver layers to match full-attention sender layers improves performance. However, for the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) variant (PLatour-SFT), C2Cs layer matching strategy (Fu et al., 2026), pairing the receivers layers with the final sender layers, works better in SFT but not GRPO. Thus, we adopt them in all SFT training. In addition, linear projection layer performs better than two-layer linear projector and two-layer MLP. We think linear projection may have enough expressiveness when pre-trained models share similar representation space (Huh et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026), and are easier for optimization especially in the direct GRPO training. Moreover, we find that initialization plays an important role here because zero-initialization makes the initial receivers behavior the same. More details are discussed in Appendix F.

sections.title: F Additional Ablations and Analysis
sections.content: F.1 More on Layer Matching We compare two layer-matching strategies in more detail: relative-depth matching distributes receiver layers across the senders depth, whereas last-n matching aligns the final sender layers with the receiver layers. As shown in Table A12, last-n matching improves PLatour-SFT performance on ARC-C, MMLURedux, and GSM8K for both sender sizes. The Chemistry results are mixed: last-n matching improves CoT performance with the 235B sender but reduces both no-CoT and CoT performance with the 8B sender. For the 235B-to-1.7B GSM8K GRPO experiment, relative-depth matching achieves 89.35%, exceeding last-n matching by 2.85 percentage points. Moreover, in the Qwen3.5-122B Qwen3.5-4B setting, Table A11 reports similar accuracies for the two strategies (90.75 and 91.25), while Table A13 shows that relative-depth (full-to-full) matching reaches high accuracy earlier in training. These results suggest that the effectiveness of layer matching depends on both the task and the training objective.

All scores are avg@4, reported as percentages. F.2 Hidden-State versus KV Transfer Table A14 compares hidden-state and KV transfer using Qwen3-8B sender and Qwen3-1.7B receiver. We replace C2Cs original projector with linear maps, using either separate or shared projections for keys and values. This change alone does not improve accuracy. Zero initialization substantially improves both variants, bringing them close to, but still below, the standalone receiver. Enabling propagation further improves accuracy by 2.352.76 percentage points, allowing both KV-transfer variants to outperform the standalone receiver. Nevertheless, PLatour-SFT remains ahead by 1.251.40 points. One possible advantage of hidden-state transfer is that it learns single mapping before the receiver constructs its keys and values through its pretrained projections. This couples the transferred information through common hidden representation, whereas separate KV mappings learn the two transformations independently. To investigate whether sharing projection parameters alone explains the gap, we also tie the key and value projection weights. This produces only small accuracy changes and does not close the gap with PLatour-SFT, suggesting that parameter sharing alone is insufficient to explain the advantage of hidden-state transfer.

F.3.1 KV-Lingo Ablations The original KV-Lingo training recipe differs from that of PLatour-SFT in its learning-rate schedule (cosine rather than linear decay) and warmup ratio (5% rather than 10%). We first evaluate the effect of adopting the PLatour-SFT recipe on answer-only tasks. As shown in Table A16, this change provides no consistent benefit, reducing accuracy in five of the six senderbenchmark combinations. Nevertheless, we retain this recipe for subsequent KV-Lingo ablations to align the optimization settings with those of C2C and PLatour-SFT. We next replace KV-Lingos KL-divergence loss with cross-entropy (CE). The KL objective is intended to preserve the receivers behavior while adapting to the senders KV caches, whereas CE directly optimizes the likelihood of target responses. Relative to the recipe-only variant, CE improves accuracy on all three answer-only benchmarks for both sender sizes. In the Qwen3-8B Qwen3-1.7B setting, it outperforms both C2C and PLatour-SFT on all three benchmarks. However, the CE variant remains below the receiver-alone baseline on every generation benchmark for both sender sizes, with particularly severe degradation in the Qwen3-235B Qwen3-1.7B setting. We hypothesize that using receiver-generated rollouts as SFT targets may contribute to this limitation, although out ablations do not isolate this factor. Finally, we examine KV-Lingos use of direct KV-cache replacement by replacing residual addition in PLatour-SFT with this mechanism, yielding the PLatour-SFT Replace variant. Compared with PLatourSFT, replacement improves accuracy on all three answer-only benchmarks with the 8B sender, but reduces accuracy on ARC-C and Chemistry with the 235B sender, while improving MMLU-Redux. On generation tasks, replacement consistently underperforms PLatour-SFT for both sender sizes, with especially large drops on GSM8K and MATH500 with the 235B sender. We hypothesize that the larger senderreceiver capacity gap makes it harder for the linear-regression initialization to align their KV representations adequately, leaving direct replacement more vulnerable to representation mismatch. Taken together, these ablations favor CE over KL for answer-only tasks and residual addition over direct KV-cache replacement for generation tasks, with the latter advantage being particularly pronounced when the senderreceiver capacity gap is large. 30 Method / Recipe ARC-C MMLU-Redux Chemistry Chemistry (Gen) GSM8K MATH500 Receiver-Alone 74.23 53.96 39.05 41.43 80.86 73.
